essentialQuestion.source: How can you tell if a photo, video or voice is real?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you know whether a photo, video or voice is real?

learningGoal.source: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, and check the source before you trust or share one.
learningGoal.back: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, and check the source before trusting or sharing one.

read.sections.0.heading.source: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI can make pictures, videos and voices

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly for art, films or education, and explain that AI made the work. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”. Someone else posted a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. Is it real?
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from a very large number of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly for art, films or education, and explain that the work was made by AI. Fake content is different: it pretends to show something real that never actually happened. A deepfake is fake content that copies the face or voice of a real person, often to trick people for money or attention. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a video of a talking goat with the caption “Made with AI, only for laughs”. Someone else posted a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. Is that photo real?
read.sections.0.text.note: "A fake" (noun) became "konten palsu" (fake content), since "palsu" is an adjective; the glossary word is "palsu". "Deepfake" kept, as Komdigi and Indonesian media do.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Some AI tools make new pictures, videos and voices. They learned from lots of real examples. So the new ones look realistic. Some people say openly that AI made their art or lessons. A fake is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. In Greenhill, the comedy club's talking goat says AI made it. But is the huge pumpkin real?
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Some AI tools make new pictures, videos and voices. Those tools learned from very many real examples. So what they make looks realistic. Some people say openly that AI made their art or lessons. Fake content is different. Fake content shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. In Greenhill, the comedy club's talking goat has a caption saying AI made it. But is the giant pumpkin real?

read.sections.1.heading.source: Strange details are clues, not proof
read.sections.1.heading.back: Strange details are clues, not proof

read.sections.1.text.source: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study, participants wrongly labelled about one in four real photographs as AI-made. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says a phone took it.
read.sections.1.text.back: Pictures made by AI sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign, or a background that merges into a wall. In a video, the mouth's movement may not fit the words. These details can be clues, but not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake picture can look perfect. Real photos can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken where there is not enough light. In a 2025 study, participants wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made. The fruit seller's photo shows very smooth skin, but the photo club says it was taken with a phone.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, people looked at real photos. They called about one in four of them AI-made. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But a phone took that photo.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Pictures made by AI sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can also look strange, if they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, people looked at real photos. They called about one in four of those photos AI-made. The fruit seller's skin is very smooth. But that photo was taken with a phone.

read.sections.2.text.source: The most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? The farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, so that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market's own page, and other people posted the same rain, so it is probably real. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.text.back: The most useful check is checking the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? The farm's own official page says they did not grow a giant pumpkin, so that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market's own official page, and other people posted the same rain, so that photo is probably real. For a voice message, contact the person another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her directly. If you still can't be sure, say so, and don't share it yet.

Don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: So check the source. Who sent that post? When? Where did it first come from? Do people you trust show the same thing? The farm says it has no giant pumpkin. So that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market itself. Other people posted the same rain. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number. So ask her directly. Not sure yet? watch.summary.source: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
watch.summary.back: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. Pictures made by AI can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In videos made by AI, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check whether the lip movement fits the words. For voices made by AI, listen to the tone of voice and the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, such as a search that finds where else a picture appears on the internet. But these tools are not always right. A human still needs to think and check before sharing.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and copied voices in scams (for example a phone call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). This lesson uses silly examples on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says fake content was made about them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner organisation's child protection procedure.

educatorNotes.0.source: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether other trusted sources show the same thing, and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. In a 2025 study (Kamali and others, CHI '25), people correctly called real photographs real 74% of the time, so about one in four were wrongly called AI-made. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer; the activity has no score. Paper version: the six posts on cards, sorted under the four headings.
educatorNotes.0.back: Teach how to check first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether other trusted sources show the same thing, and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual oddities (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, not proof: newer tools make them less and less often, and real photos can also show strange details. In a 2025 study (Kamali and colleagues, CHI '25), people correctly called real photos real 74% of the time, so about one in four were wrongly called AI-made. Accept “can't be confirmed yet” as a strong answer; the activity has no score. Paper version: the six posts on cards, grouped under the four headings.

educatorNotes.1.source: Labelled AI work (art, films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
educatorNotes.1.back: AI work with a caption (art, films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as fake content that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Captions can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a captioned post can mislead if shared without its caption. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one example that has been checked; learners don't need to go online.
